units.title: Mitosis and meiosis foundations
units.why: Cell division enables growth, repair and the production of reproductive cells.
principles: mitosis produces genetically similar diploid cells
meiosis halves chromosome number and creates variation
misconceptions: meiosis is simply two identical mitoses
solutions: mitosis two similar; meiosis four varied

videoPackage.title: Division with purpose
videoPackage.transcript: We follow chromosome behaviour through mitosis and meiosis and connect chromosome number to growth and reproduction.

units.title: Plant tissues and transport
units.why: Plant structures distribute water, minerals and sugars while supporting growth.
principles: xylem carries water and minerals upward
stomata regulate gas exchange and water loss
examples: guard cells open and close stomata
solutions: xylem dead tubes; phloem living sieve tubes

videoPackage.title: Transport in plants
videoPackage.transcript: We trace water from root hairs through xylem and sugars through phloem, then connect stomata to gas exchange and water loss.

units.title: Ecosystems and biodiversity
units.why: Ecology explains interdependence and how biodiversity supports resilient environments.
misconceptions: energy cycles in the same way as matter

videoPackage.title: Energy through ecosystems
videoPackage.transcript: We map who eats whom, follow energy loss between trophic levels, and distinguish cycling matter from one-way energy flow.

units.title: Support and transport systems
units.why: Human systems work together to move substances, support movement and maintain life.
principles: surface area and thin barriers aid exchange
examples: alveoli provide large surface for diffusion
red blood cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin
misconceptions: blood is only a transport fluid

videoPackage.title: Systems working together
videoPackage.transcript: We connect support, transport and gas exchange, showing how structure and scale make human systems efficient.

units.title: Inheritance and genetic crosses
units.why: Genetics explains variation, inheritance patterns and responsible interpretation of traits.
examples: A recessive phenotype requires two recessive alleles
misconceptions: dominant means more common or stronger
practice: Why carriers show no recessive trait?

videoPackage.title: Predicting inheritance
videoPackage.transcript: We separate alleles into gametes, combine them in a Punnett square, and interpret expected genotype and phenotype ratios carefully.
